title: Create or Modify System Process: Systemd Service
shortTitle: Create or Modify System Process: Systemd Service
summary: Systemd is the service manager and init system on most modern Linux distributions, and it is driven entirely by unit configuration files, most of them ending in .service. System level units live under the system directories below /, typically /etc/systemd/system and /usr/lib/systemd/system, while user units live under the user's home directory. Within a unit, ExecStart, ExecStartPre, and ExecStartPost run when the service starts, whether that is at boot or from systemctl start; ExecReload runs on restart; ExecStop, ExecStopPre, and ExecStopPost run on stop. That last group matters because a unit can look quiet at boot yet fire when an administrator tries to stop it, turning routine maintenance into a re-infection. The same unit can elevate privileges in two ways: the User directive can name a more powerful account, and systemd generators can build or rewrite units at boot from non-native configuration, so the visible unit may not be the file the attacker actually controls. Detection therefore combines unit file creation and modification events, symlinks into unit directories, journal entries showing a unit starting and immediately exiting, and process lineage in which a unit execs a binary from a temporary or home directory rather than a packaged path.

beginner.definition: Systemd is the part of Linux that starts services when the computer boots. A service is a program that runs in the background, such as a web server or a print spooler. This technique is when an attacker creates or edits the file that describes such a service, so their program starts too.
beginner.whyItMatters: A service file is read at every boot, so the attacker's program comes back even after a restart. Service files also name the account the program runs as, which lets the attacker pick a powerful one. Many defenders rarely look at these files, so the change can sit unnoticed for months. It is a quiet and reliable way to keep access.
howItWorks: The attacker writes a unit file, usually ending in .service, and places it in a systemd unit directory.
The file lists the program to run in its ExecStart directive, and often a friendly description as cover.
A link or symbolic reference inside the unit folder can point to a payload stored elsewhere on the disk.
They then enable the unit, so systemd starts that program automatically during every boot.
Some directives run on stop or reload, so a service can also execute code when it is shut down.
The User directive can be set so the program runs as a more powerful account than the one that created it.
beginner.example: Picture an apartment building with a board by the entrance listing the caretaker's daily jobs. A resident adds a neat new line, asking the caretaker to open the basement each morning at seven. The caretaker follows the board without question, because it is the official list. Nobody in the building notices until someone reads the board entry by entry.
takeaways: On Linux, a .service unit file is the main place to look for this kind of persistence.
Some directives run when a service stops, so stopping a suspicious service is not always safe.
The User directive decides whose rights the program gets, which is how privilege escalation happens.

objectives: Explain the role of systemd on a modern Linux host.
Describe how a .service unit file triggers execution at boot.
Name the directives that run on start, reload, and stop.
Explain how the User directive can raise an attacker's privileges.
Explain what systemd generators are and why they complicate review.
